list.listitem: Diagnosis of hydrocele can be made by examination; order ultrasound if any uncertainty exists that hydrocele is the sole pathology. C
Asymptomatic noncommunicating hydroceles can safely go untreated. C
Communicating or symptomatic hydroceles can be treated by surgical resection or aspiration and sclerotherapy. B

background.definition: A hydrocele is a fluid collection in the scrotum between the layers of the tunica vaginalis. A communicating hydrocele represents a patent processus vaginalis allowing fluid to cross from the peritoneal space into the scrotum.

list.listitem: Incidence of neonatal hydrocele is as high as 4.7% of neonates undergoing circumcision.
Approximately 1% of adult males have hydroceles.
Congenital
Infection (epididymitis, orchitis, or tropical infections; eg, filariasis)
Trauma
Complication of scrotal surgery (ie, vasectomy)
Testicular torsion
Tumor

Congenital hydroceles noted within the first year of life are caused by delayed or incomplete closure of the processus vaginalis. The same mechanism may contribute to hydroceles occurring later in life.
In acquired hydroceles, the cause is more likely to be an obstruction of venous or lymphatic drainage or an inflammatory process such as infection.
Hydroceles can be diagnosed by physical examination, if a smooth cystic mass that easily transilluminates is identified adjacent to the testis. C
Scrotal ultrasound should be ordered if the testis is not fully palpable or if an abnormality other than hydrocele is suspected based on history or physical examination. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Soft mass in the scrotum protruding from the inguinal canal
Smooth, spherical cysts often located on the epididymis
Tortuous spermatic vein with "bag of worms" consistency, usually left sided
Painful engorgement of the epididymis often associated with dysuria
Painless, firm, irregular mass on the surface of the testis
Abrupt onset severe pain with "bell clapper" deformity and loss of cremasteric reflex

list.listitem: Hydroceles typically present with a history of a tense, nonpainful scrotal mass but can present with scrotal discomfort or back pain.
Because they are cystic structures, hydroceles transilluminate easily.
If the fluid collection is large enough, it often encompasses the testicle, making it difficult or impossible to feel the testis itself.

In communicating hydroceles, the mass may reduce in size with the patient supine. On the basis of patient history, this may present as a scrotal mass that increases in size throughout the day and shrinks overnight.

Scrotal ultrasound is the standard diagnostic tool. In addition to confirming the diagnosis of hydrocele, it can evaluate other scrotal structures and determine whether there is a causative agent such as a tumor. Ultrasound can also evaluate for an inguinal hernia, which often accompanies a hydrocele in the newborn.

Ten percent of testicular tumors present with a reactive hydrocele. If the hydrocele does not completely transilluminate or if there is any doubt about the makeup of a scrotal mass including the inability to fully palpate the testis, confirm the diagnosis with scrotal ultrasound.
Scrotal ultrasound should be ordered to rule out other scrotal pathology unless a hydrocele is asymptomatic and associated with a fully palpable, normal testicle.
Infants and children with hydroceles can be safely observed for up to 2 years to see whether the hydrocele will resolve spontaneously.
Asymptomatic noncommunicating hydroceles can safely go untreated. C

Communicating or symptomatic hydroceles can be treated by surgical resection or aspiration and sclerotherapy. The latter may be slightly less effective but is less expensive, has lower postoperative complications, and may result to faster work resumption. B
No surgical repair is necessary for a noncommunicating hydrocele that is asymptomatic if the testicle is normal. If the hydrocele is symptomatic or if it communicates, surgery is warranted.
Communicating hydroceles are repaired in a similar fashion to indirect hernias, as the anatomical defect is essentially the same.
Noncommunicating hydroceles can be treated with either aspiration and sclerotherapy with sodium tetradecyl sulfate (a minimally invasive technique) or surgical resection.

A nonrandomized trial compared aspiration and sclerotherapy in 27 patients with surgical resection in 24 patients. Surgical resection was slightly more effective (84% vs 76% overall success and 75% vs 87% patient satisfaction) but had a higher rate of complications (40% vs 8%, mostly hematoma) and was significantly more expensive than aspiration and sclerotherapy. A subsequent randomized trial of 60 adult men with hydrocele randomized to hydrocelectomy or aspiration and sclerotherapy confirmed these findings, with a greater risk of recurrence with aspiration and sclerotherapy (35%) but fewer complications, less morbidity, and lower cost.

A Cochrane review of 4 RCTs involving 275 patients with 282 hydroceles noted that aspiration and sclerotherapy, compared to hydrocelectomy, may be cheaper, result in fewer postoperative complications, and may lead to faster work resumption but may have a higher recurrence rate. In the short-term, the cure rate appear comparable for the two methods. Due to high study heterogeneity, there is considerable uncertainty in these findings.

Surgical options for noncommunicating hydroceles include an inguinal or scrotal approach, with similar results in the two groups. Children should undergo surgery with the inguinal approach because of the increased risk of a patent processus vaginalis.

Surgical complications most commonly included recurrence, hematoma, and infection. In 1 study of scrotal surgeries performed for benign conditions, complications included recurrence, hematoma, and infection. The overall complication rate for the study was 20%. Patients undergoing hydrocelectomy represented 55% of the patients and 95% of the complications.
Children older than 2 years or children younger than 2 years in whom a concomitant hernia cannot be ruled out are typical pediatric surgical candidates and should be referred for evaluation.
Referral is warranted for all communicating hydroceles. Referral is warranted for older children and adults with symptomatic hydroceles.
Hydroceles may progressively enlarge, but as long as they remain asymptomatic, no treatment is necessary in adults with no causative pathology. C

Noncommunicating hydroceles in infants often resolve spontaneously in the first 2 years. New onset hydroceles in boys over the age of 1 year also resolve in about 75% of cases in 2 years, with an average time of less than 6 months.B
See "When to refer and hospitalize" section.
